1H (Number Theory)

Words: 174 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 174
1H OurBigBook.com
For every odd prime p and n≥1, the group of units modulo an integer (Z/pnZ)× is a cyclic group, of order φ(pn)=pn−1(p−1); a generator is a primitive root.
Modulo seven, 3,32,…,36 are 3,2,6,4,5,1, so three has order six. Moreover 36−1=728=7⋅104 is divisible by seven exactly once. We prove the lifting needed here. If u=1+7rv with r≥1 and 7∤v, the binomial expansion gives u7=1+7r+1v+O(7r+2), so v7​(u7−1)=r+1. Induction therefore gives
v7​(36⋅7j−1)=j+1.
(1)
Any exponent giving one modulo 7n is divisible by six. The order also divides 6⋅7n−1 by Lagrange theorem, while the displayed valuation rules out each proper divisor of this form. Consequently three is a primitive root modulo every 7n.
Since 23=1(mod7) and two is not one, its order modulo seven is three. A generator modulo 7n would reduce to a generator modulo seven, because reduction is a surjective group homomorphism. Thus two is never a primitive root modulo 7n. Finally every unit modulo eight is odd, and (2k+1)2=1+4k(k+1)≡1(mod8). All unit orders are at most two, whereas the unit group has four elements. There is no primitive root modulo eight.

2G (Topics in Analysis)

Words: 165 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 165
2G OurBigBook.com
The Brouwer fixed-point theorem says that every continuous map from a closed Euclidean ball to itself has a fixed point. For the closed disc D⊂R2 its equivalent no-retraction theorem says that there is no continuous r:D→∂D satisfying r(z)=z on ∂D.
Assume the fixed-point theorem and suppose such a retraction exists. Then F(x)=−r(x) maps D continuously into itself. A fixed point must lie on the boundary, where r(x)=x, giving x=−x, impossible on the unit circle.
Conversely suppose F:D→D is continuous and has no fixed point. From F(x) draw the ray through x and let r(x) be its exit point on the circle. To check continuity rather than merely relying on the picture, put v=x−F(x)=0. The exit point is F(x)+t(x)v, where
t(x)=∣v∣2−F(x)⋅v+(F(x)⋅v)2+(1−∣F(x)∣2)∣v∣2​​.
(2)
This is continuous, lies on the circle and has t(x)≥1. On the boundary the exit point is x, so r is a retraction, contradicting the assumed theorem. Hence the two disc formulations are equivalent; the same argument works for a ball in any dimension.

4G (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 275 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 275
4G OurBigBook.com
A binary linear-feedback shift register of length L keeps L bits and produces a sequence satisfying a recurrence
sn​+c1​sn−1​+⋯+cL​sn−L​=0in F2​.
(5)
After each output it shifts its stored bits and inserts the feedback bit. Its connection polynomial is C(z)=1+c1​z+⋯+cL​zL. This convention reverses the usual characteristic polynomial zL+c1​zL−1+⋯+cL​.
The Berlekamp-Massey algorithm recovers the shortest recurrence compatible with observed bits. Maintain the current C, length L, an earlier polynomial B that last caused a length increase, and the offset m since that increase. Initially C=B=1,L=0,m=1. At position n calculate the discrepancy d=sn​+∑j=1L​cj​sn−j​. If d=0, advance m. If d=1, save T=C and replace C by C+zmB. If also 2L≤n, replace L by n+1−L, B by T and m by one; otherwise increase m. Over a general field the correction is (d/b)zmB, where b is the saved nonzero discrepancy. The correction cancels the failed equation while retaining the previous successful ones; when it forces a length increase the smallest possible new length is n+1−L.
Here, indexing the first bit by zero, the nonzero discrepancies occur at positions 1,4,6. The corresponding updates are
(C,L)=(1+z2,2),(1+z2+z3,3),(1+z3+z4,4).
(6)
Every subsequent supplied discrepancy is zero. Thus
C(z)=1+z3+z4,sn​=sn−3​+sn−4​.​
(7)
Equivalently the characteristic feedback polynomial is z4+z+1. No length-three recurrence works: positions 3,4,5 force c2​=1,c1​=0,c3​=1, but position six then has nonzero discrepancy. The recovered length is therefore minimal. Observing at least twice the true linear complexity ordinarily identifies the recurrence, after which a known consecutive block determines all future key bits. This is why a bare register is unsuitable as a cryptographic keystream generator; a finite prefix alone does not exclude a longer generator that later diverges.

The probability generating function encodes the population distribution in one analytic function. Its coefficients and derivative recover
P(n,t)=n!1​∂sn​ϕ(0,t),⟨n⟩=∂s​ϕ(1,t),
(11)
provided the mean is finite. Higher derivatives at one give factorial moments, and normalization says ϕ(1,t)=1.
Interpret the supplied birth and death expressions as transition rates: over a small time dt their probabilities are (α+βn)dt+o(dt) and γndt+o(dt). Incoming probability from n−1 and n+1, minus both outgoing rates, gives
∂t​P(n,t)=(α+β(n−1))P(n−1,t)+γ(n+1)P(n+1,t)−[α+(β+γ)n]P(n,t),
(12)
with P(−1,t)=0. Multiplying by sn and summing yields
ϕt​=α(s−1)ϕ+(s−1)(βs−γ)ϕs​.​
(13)
At stationarity, ϕs​/ϕ=α/(γ−βs), so integration and normalization give
ϕ(s)=(γ−βsγ−β​)α/β,⟨n⟩=γ−βα​.​
(14)
Alternatively differentiating the evolution equation at one gives m′=α−(γ−β)m, so m(t)=α/(γ−β)+[m(0)−α/(γ−β)]e−(γ−β)t. If β=0, the displayed power expression is understood in its limit: ϕ(s)=e(α/γ)(s−1), a Poisson distribution with mean α/γ.

7E OurBigBook.com
Solving the two factors in each equation gives (0,0),(3,0),(0,3),(1,1). The Jacobian is
Df=(2x+2y−3−2y​2x3−2x−2y​).
(15)
At the three boundary equilibria its eigenvalues are 3,−3. These equilibria are hyperbolic fixed points; the Hartman-Grobman theorem gives local topological conjugacy to their saddle linearizations. At (1,1) the matrix is (1−2​2−1​), with eigenvalues ±i3​. The linearization is a centre, but the hyperbolic theorem does not apply there.
The nonlinear classification follows from the actual Hamiltonian
H(x,y)=xy(x+y−3),x˙=Hy​,y˙​=−Hx​.​
(16)
Along solutions H˙=Hx​Hy​−Hy​Hx​=0. At (1,1), H=−1 and its Hessian is (21​12​), which is positive definite. Nearby regular level curves are closed ovals around this strict minimum. Their vector field is nonzero and tangent, so each is a periodic orbit. The nonlinear equilibrium is a centre.
The separatrix level H=0 consists of x=0, y=0, and x+y=3. Within the triangle they connect the saddles as (3,0)→(0,0)→(0,3)→(3,0). The interior levels −1<H<0 are nested clockwise periodic orbits; outside the triangle the remaining level branches are unbounded. On y=0, flow is left for 0<x<3 and right for x<0 or x>3; on x=0, it is up for 0<y<3 and down otherwise. These directions and the invariant levels determine the full phase portrait.

Use the one-sided Laplace transform F(s)=∫0∞​e−stf(t)dt. Since f=0 on [0,1), substitution gives L[f(t+1)](s)=esF(s). Thus
F(s)=s(es−1/2)1​=s(1−e−s/2)2e−s​.
(17)
Its poles are s=0 and sn​=−log2+2πin, with residues of estF(s) respectively two and 2esn​t/sn​. For t>1 close the Bromwich inversion formula to the left, using horizontal heights avoiding those poles. The left-side integrand decays like est/s, and on the right-side horizontal ends like es(t−1)/s, so the added integrals vanish with the usual symmetric limiting contour. The residue theorem gives
f(t)=2+21−tn=−∞∑∞​2πin−log2e2πint​(t≥1),​
(18)
where the series is summed symmetrically and at jumps has the midpoint value.
For t<1 the vanishing can be checked directly in the inversion integral, rather than inferred from the recurrence. On any vertical line ℜs=c>0 expand the denominator geometrically, uniformly there:
F(s)=2∑j=0∞​2−jse−(j+1)s​.
(19)
Each inversion term is 21−j(2πi)−1∫c−i∞c+i∞​es(t−j−1)ds/s. If t<1, close this contour to the right: the exponential decays, and the pole at zero is outside, so every term is zero. Equivalently the geometric expansion bounds the full closing contour by the same decaying factors. Thus f(t)=0 for t<1.
The same integral gives f(t)=2∑j≥0​2−jH(t−j−1) elsewhere. For m<t<m+1 with integer m≥1, this is 4(1−2−m), which directly verifies the difference equation. Neither a Laplace transform nor a Fourier series determines values at isolated jumps; the printed series fixes the standard convention H(0)=1/2, including f(1)=1.

y˙​=MJMT∇y​K.

A comoving coordinate χ labels a galaxy carried by the homogeneous cosmological flow. Its physical separation at time t is r(t)=a(t)χ, where a is the scale factor. Thus v=a˙χ=(a˙/a)r, the Hubble law, apart from peculiar velocities relative to this flow. In particular
H0​=a(t0​)a˙(t0​)​.​
(23)

b OurBigBook.com
Assume the present universe is expanding, a˙(t0​)>0. The stated energy inequality and the Raychaudhuri equation imply a¨≤0 wherever a>0. Therefore for t<t0​ in that positive branch, a˙(t)≥a˙(t0​), and
a(t0​)−a(t)=∫tt0​​a˙(s)ds≥(t0​−t)a˙(t0​).
(24)
Nonnegativity of a(t) forces t0​−t≤a(t0​)/a˙(t0​)=H0−1​. If the solution remains valid towards the past, its positive branch must thus end in a=0 within that time; a positive scale factor extending further would contradict the inequality. Hence
t0​−ti​≤H0−1​.​
(25)
This argument presumes an expanding branch and the stated energy condition throughout it, rather than proving either assumption.
There are two relevant failures of the naive numerical bound. The supplied ten-billion-year Hubble time is an approximate observational input: a smaller inferred present expansion rate gives a larger Hubble time, and comparison with stellar ages must include these uncertainties. More decisively, a positive cosmological constant, or other dark energy with sufficiently negative pressure, has ρ+3P/c2<0 and permits accelerated expansion, so the concavity assumption fails. Observations of acceleration therefore remove this particular upper-bound argument. This is a discussion of the supplied historical estimate, not an assertion that its numerical value is a current measurement.

Parametrize the circle by z=eit, 0≤t≤2π. Choose a continuous argument ϑ(t) of ϕ(eit), so ϕ(eit)=∣ϕ(eit)∣eiϑ(t). Its winding number about zero is
w(ϕ)=2πϑ(2π)−ϑ(0)​∈Z.
(26)
The two facts proved below determine the requested calculation without needing differentiability or contour integration. Put P(z)=(3z−2)(z−3)(2z+1). On ∣z∣=1, ∣P(z)∣≥1⋅2⋅1=2, so adding one does not change its winding. The first and third factors have winding one, since their constant terms have modulus smaller than their linear terms; the second has winding zero, since its z term has modulus smaller than its constant term. Nonzero constants have winding zero and z has winding one. Thus
w(ϕ)=1+0+1=2.​
(27)

12F (Geometry and Groups)

Words: 283 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 283
12F OurBigBook.com
In curvature-minus-one polar coordinates the hyperbolic metric is ds2=dr2+sinh2rdθ2. Thus the area element is sinhrdrdθ, giving
AreaB(r)=2π(coshr−1)=4πsinh2(r/2).​
(30)
It is asymptotic to πer.
For a usual locally finite tessellation with compact congruent tiles of nonempty interior, let their diameter be at most D and choose in each a congruently placed interior ball of radius r0​>0. These balls have disjoint interiors. The number of tiles meeting a geodesic segment of length one is uniformly bounded: their ball centres lie in a ball of radius D+1, and the disjoint r0​-balls lie in the larger ball of radius D+1+r0​. Comparing areas supplies a constant K. A path of length R, divided into at most ⌈R⌉ such segments, therefore crosses at most K(⌈R⌉+1) tiles. A small generic perturbation avoids vertices if steps are defined by crossing sides.
Consequently the union of tiles at most n steps from the initial tile contains a metric ball of radius cn−C for fixed c>0,C. If A is tile area, their number N(n) is at least AreaB(cn−C)/A, an exponential lower bound. Conversely any chain of n adjacent tiles lies in B(D(n+1)) about a point in the initial tile; the interiors are disjoint, so AN(n)≤AreaB(D(n+1)). Thus N(n) is bounded above and below by positive exponential functions of n. No precise common growth exponent is claimed.
An explicit example is the regular right-angled pentagon tiling {5,4}: reflect a regular hyperbolic pentagon with all angles π/2 in its sides. Four pentagons meet at each vertex, and their interiors tile the plane. Its tiles have area 3π−5π/2=π by the hyperbolic polygon area formula. The compactness and ordinary local finiteness assumptions exclude pathological decompositions with degenerate tiles.

The fitted grouped-binomial logistic regression generalized linear model treats seasonal hits Hi​ as independent Bin(ni​,pi​) variables, with ni​=ABi​ and
log1−pi​pi​​=β0​+β1​ai​+β2​ai2​.
(31)
Thus the response supplied to glm is a proportion, and weights=AB supplies its binomial denominator; it is not a regression with equally precise seasonal averages. I(Age^2) forms the numerical square rather than using a formula operator. The estimates maximize ℓ(β)=∑i​[Hi​ηi​−ni​log(1+eηi​)] up to a constant, where ηi​=xiT​β, xi​=(1,ai​,ai2​)T.
The observed negative Hessian is XTWX, Wii​=ni​p​i​(1−p​i​). Expanding the score around the true parameter and applying a central-limit approximation gives β​≈N(β,(XTWX)−1). The reported standard errors are square roots of the diagonal entries of this inverse; the binomial dispersion is fixed at one. Each z value divides the coefficient estimate by its standard error, and the reported two-sided Wald test uses a standard normal approximation under the corresponding zero-coefficient hypothesis.
The last line reports the deviance against the saturated model,
D=2∑i​[Hi​logni​p​i​Hi​​+(ni​−Hi​)logni​(1−p​i​)ni​−Hi​​],
(32)
with 0log0=0. There are 22 seasonal observations and three fitted parameters, so 19 degrees of freedom. Under the quadratic-logit model, independent binomial sampling and sufficiently large expected counts, D≈χ192​. The value 23.345 gives an upper-tail probability about 0.22, no evidence of lack of fit at conventional levels. This approximation and the independence assumption should not be confused with an exact test of a player's ability.
The final commands recover the coefficients, apply the inverse logit p=(1+e−η)−1, plot the observed averages against age, and join the fitted probabilities at the observed ages. The fitted curve is smooth, rises towards its peak at a=−β​1​/(2β​2​)≈29.95, then falls. Its maximum is about 0.373; the early and late observed points include markedly lower averages. The plot uses equally sized points even though their binomial precisions differ.

Φ˙(t)=A(t)Φ(t),Φ(0)=I.​

The Floquet multipliers are the eigenvalues of the monodromy matrix Φ(T). Differentiating the orbit equation shows that its tangent X˙(t) solves the variational equation. Since X˙(T)=X˙(0)=0, one multiplier is one.
For an invertible fundamental matrix, differentiating the determinant gives (detΦ)′=tr(Φ−1Φ˙)detΦ=trAdetΦ. Integration from the identity yields detΦ(T)=exp(∫0T​trA(t)dt). The determinant is the product of the two multipliers, so the other is
μ=exp(∫0T​∇⋅f(X(t))dt).​

16H (Logic and Set Theory)

Words: 376 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 376
16H OurBigBook.com
A chain-complete partially ordered set has a supremum for each chain (and a least element if the empty chain is included). The weaker condition needed for Zorn lemma is that every chain have an upper bound; some terminology also calls this chain-complete. Zorn's lemma says that a nonempty partially ordered set with this upper-bound property has a maximal element. We verify that exact hypothesis below.
Consider the lattice ideals containing a but not b, ordered by inclusion. The principal ideal ↓a belongs to this family because b≰a. The union of a nonempty chain of such ideals is an ideal: two of its elements lie together in one member of the chain, which contains their join and everything below it. The union still avoids b. The empty chain has the initial principal ideal as an upper bound. Zorn supplies a maximal such ideal I.
We prove that I is a prime lattice ideal. If x,y∈/I, maximality says that the ideals generated by adjoining x and by adjoining y both contain b. Thus b≤i∨x and b≤j∨y for some i,j∈I: the first generated ideal consists of elements below i∨x, and similarly for y. If x∧y∈I, distributivity gives
b≤(i∨x)∧(j∨y)=(i∧j)∨(i∧y)∨(x∧j)∨(x∧y)∈I,
(45)
a contradiction. Consequently x∧y∈I implies x∈I or y∈I.
Define f(x)=0 on I and one elsewhere. An ideal contains x∨y exactly when it contains both x and y, and its primeness says that it contains x∧y exactly when it contains at least one of them. Thus f preserves both joins and meets, and f(a)=0,f(b)=1 as required.
For completeness, take the Lindenbaum algebra of classical propositional formulae modulo provable equivalence, including any given premises as axioms. It is a Boolean, hence distributive, lattice; provable implication is its order. If a formula P is not provable from the premises, then 1≰[P]. The separation just proved, with a=[P],b=1, gives a homomorphism of lattices sending P to zero and one to one. It also sends zero to zero, since 0≤[P], and preserves complements because their meet is zero and join is one. Its values on atomic propositions form a Boolean valuation satisfying all premises and falsifying P. Thus semantic consequence implies provability, the completeness theorem for propositional logic.

For a finite connected plane graph, with v vertices, e edges and f faces including the unbounded face, Euler formula for a connected planar graph is
v−e+f=2.​
(46)
If the graph is a tree, e=v−1 and f=1. Otherwise remove an edge on a cycle. This preserves connectivity and joins the two faces on its sides, so both e and f decrease by one. Repeating reaches a tree, preserving v−e+f throughout and proving the formula.
For a simple connected graph with v≥3, each face boundary walk has length at least three, with bridges counted twice in the walk; the sum of lengths is 2e. Hence 3f≤2e, which with Euler gives e≤3v−6. If it has no triangles in a graph, no face boundary walk can have length three, and every boundary length is at least four. Thus 4f≤2e, giving
e≤2v−4for a triangle-free planar graph with v≥3.​
(47)
For a disconnected graph, add noncrossing bridges between its components; this preserves simplicity and creates no triangles, reducing to the connected bound.
Every triangle-free planar graph with at least three vertices has average degree 2e/v<4, and therefore a vertex of degree at most three. Remove one such vertex. Its remaining graph is again triangle-free and planar. Induction, with graphs on at most two vertices as the base cases, provides a graph colouring with four colours of the remainder. At most three colours appear on the removed vertex's neighbours, so a fourth colour extends the graph colouring. This proves four-colourability without using the four-colour theorem.

Let L be the splitting field of the separable polynomial. Its Galois group is G=AutK​(L), acting faithfully on its n distinct roots, hence as a subgroup of Sn​. An automorphism preserves each root's minimal polynomial. Conversely an isomorphism K(α)→K(β) for roots of the same irreducible factor extends to an embedding of L in an algebraic closure, and normality of the splitting field makes the image L itself. Thus the root orbits are precisely the irreducible factors' root sets. The action is transitive exactly when the polynomial is irreducible.
If n=p is prime, a transitive action has p∣∣G∣ by orbit-stabilizer, so Cauchy theorem for groups supplies an element of order p. Its permutation must be a p-cycle. Conversely a p-cycle already acts transitively on all p roots. This proves the stated equivalence for prime degree.
The factorization theorem modulo a good prime says that if an integer polynomial retains its degree and has square-free reduction modulo p, and that reduction's irreducible factor degrees are d1​,…,dr​, its Galois group over Q contains a permutation with disjoint cycle lengths d1​,…,dr​. Equivalently the finite-field Galois group, generated by Frobenius on the roots, occurs as an unramified decomposition subgroup. The degree-retention qualification matters for nonmonic polynomials.
For the given quintic, Eisenstein criterion at three proves irreducibility. Modulo two it factors as
x5+x+1=(x2+x+1)(x3+x2+1).
(48)
Neither factor has a root in F2​, so both are irreducible, and they are distinct; the reduction is separable. Thus G contains an element of cycle type (2)(3), whose cube is a transposition. It is also transitive of degree five.
To prove that this forces the full symmetric group here, form the graph on the five roots with an edge for each conjugate in G of that transposition. The graph is G-invariant, and transitivity makes its connected components all the same size. That size divides five; there is an edge, so the size cannot be one. Hence the graph is connected. Transpositions along the edges of a connected graph generate all transpositions (move along a path and conjugate successive swaps), and hence generate S5​. They all belong to G, giving
G=S5​.​
(49)

Two norms are Lipschitz equivalent norms if constants c,C>0 satisfy c∥u∥1​≤∥u∥2​≤C∥u∥1​ for every u. On the vector space of finitely supported sequences, the norms ∥x∥1​=∑∣xi​∣ and ∥x∥∞​=max∣xi​∣ are not equivalent: a vector with N entries equal to one has the two norms N and one.
For dimension d<∞, choose a basis and write u=∑xi​ei​. Any norm satisfies ∥u∥≤∑∣xi​∣∥ei​∥≤C∣x∣2​. This also implies its continuity in the Euclidean coordinates, by ∣∥u∥−∥v∥∣≤∥u−v∥≤C∣x−y∣2​. Its positive continuous values on the compact Euclidean unit sphere have a positive minimum c. Homogeneity gives c∣x∣2​≤∥u∥, proving equivalence with the Euclidean norm and hence between any two norms.
If a finite-dimensional subspace U of a normed space contains a sequence converging in the ambient norm, its coefficient vectors are Cauchy by this equivalence. The coefficients converge in Rd or Cd, and the reconstructed vector lies in U and is the ambient limit. Thus finite-dimensional subspaces are closed.
A finite-dimensional normed space has nonempty open balls with compact closures by equivalence and Heine-Borel. Conversely let an open set O have compact closure. Choose w∈O and r>0 such that B(w,r)⊂O. Its closed ball of radius r/2 is a closed subset of the compact closure of O and is therefore compact. Translation and scaling make the closed unit ball compact.
If the space were infinite-dimensional, construct unit vectors xj​ with dist(xj​,span(x1​,…,xj−1​))>1/2. Here is the needed Riesz lemma: for a proper closed subspace M, choose z∈/M, put d=dist(z,M)>0, and choose m∈M with ∥z−m∥<2d; then (z−m)/∥z−m∥ has distance greater than 1/2 from M. The finite spans are closed by the earlier argument, so this constructs the sequence. Its members are separated by more than 1/2, and have no convergent subsequence, contradicting compactness. Therefore the space is finite-dimensional exactly when it has a nonempty open set with compact closure.

a OurBigBook.com
For the first-order quasilinear equation a(x,u)⋅∇u=b(x,u), suppose the coefficients and initial data u=g on a smooth hypersurface Σ are C1. At an initial point x0​, require a(x0​,g(x0​))⋅n(x0​)=0 for a normal n to Σ; this is precisely the condition that Σ be a non-characteristic hypersurface. Then in a neighborhood of x0​ there is a unique C1 solution taking the given data. Smooth coefficients and data give corresponding higher regularity.
The method of characteristics solves x˙=a(x,u), u˙=b(x,u) from each initial point. The non-characteristic condition makes the map from the initial coordinates and characteristic time to x locally invertible, so these characteristic solutions define the asserted function.

b

Words: 163 Articles: 1
29A OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 163
b OurBigBook.com
Characteristics satisfy dx/ds=1, dy/ds=x, du/ds=0. From (ξ,0) they are x=ξ+s, y=ξs+s2/2, u=f(ξ), so x2−2y=ξ2. The initial parameter is recovered on the two initial half-axes by
u(x,y)=f(sgn(x)x2−2y​),x=0,y<x2/2.​
(80)
This is C1 on the displayed open set, takes the prescribed data at y=0,x=0, and substitution verifies ux​+xuy​=0. Each branch may extend separately beyond this chosen domain, but arbitrary data on both half-axes need not allow one common extension.
The initial line has normal (0,1); the transport field is (1,x), whose normal component is x. Thus it is non-characteristic exactly away from the origin. At the origin the equation itself would require ux​(0,0)=f′(0)=0. For generic f this fails, so a C1 solution on a neighborhood of the entire initial line is not guaranteed. The parabola y=x2/2 is the envelope where the recovery of ξ degenerates. Characteristics can also meet both initial half-axes, imposing compatibility such as f(ξ)=f(−ξ) on an attempted larger domain.

Here dy/ds=1, dx/ds=u2, du/ds=0, so from initial parameter ξ we get y=s, x=ξ+ξ2y and u=ξ. Solving for the branch agreeing with u=x at y=0, and rationalizing the apparent division by y, gives
u(x,y)=1+1+4xy​2x​,1+4xy>0.​
(81)
This formula is smooth on that open set, which contains every point of the initial line. It satisfies x=u+yu2 and 1+2yu=1+4xy​>0. Differentiation gives ux​=1/(1+2yu), uy​=−u2/(1+2yu), verifying the equation and the data.
The transport field is (u2,1), with normal component one on y=0, so the initial line is everywhere non-characteristic. This explains why neighborhoods cover the entire initial line, although a single fixed-width strip need not work for unbounded x.

For the Laplace method, under the usual regularity (p continuous at zero and q sufficiently smooth near its isolated minimum), write q(t)=q(0)+q′′(0)t2/2+o(t2). On any interval bounded away from zero, continuity and uniqueness of the minimum give a positive gap in q, making that contribution exponentially smaller. Set t=s/x​ near zero. The leading integral is
I(x)=e−xq(0)x−1/2[p(0)∫0∞​e−q′′(0)s2/2ds+o(1)].
(82)
A local quadratic lower bound on q−q(0) justifies dominated convergence after this rescaling. Thus, when p(0)=0,
I(x)∼p(0)e−xq(0)2xq′′(0)π​​.​
(83)
If p(0)=0, the displayed coefficient vanishes and further local terms of p determine the first nonzero asymptotic term; one must not interpret a zero coefficient as an asymptotic equivalence.
For the first Bessel integral, take q(θ)=−cosθ, p(θ)=cos(νθ). The endpoint minimum is q(0)=−1, q′′(0)=1, p(0)=1, so after dividing by π its leading term is ex/2πx​.
For the second integral, cosht≥1+t2/2 gives, for fixed real ν,
​∫0∞​e−xcosht−νtdt​≤e−x∫0∞​e−xt2/2+∣ν∣tdt=O(e−xx−1/2).
(84)
Completing the square proves the last bound for large x. It is exponentially smaller than the first integral; the fixed prefactor sin(νπ) does not change this. Therefore
Iν​(x)∼2πx​ex​(x→+∞, ν fixed).​
(85)

Let E=e−ikx+k2t. Expanding ∂t​(Eq)+∂x​(EX) shows that the required flux is
X=−qx​−ikq.​
(86)
Indeed Xx​−ikX=−qxx​−k2q, cancelling the k2q from the time derivative. Introduce a potential φ by φx​=Eq, φt​=E(qx​+ikq). Equality of its mixed derivatives is precisely the conservation law. With φ=Eμ, these equations become the linear auxiliary system
μx​−ikμ=q,μt​+k2μ=qx​+ikq.​
(87)
This is a Lax pair in the affine-potential form used for linear evolution equations. If a homogeneous matrix pair is preferred, set Ψ=(μ,1)T and use Ψx​=(ik0​q0​)Ψ, Ψt​=(−k20​qx​+ikq0​)Ψ. Its zero-curvature condition has upper-right entry qt​−qxx​ and all other entries zero.

The Cole-Hopf transformation for the sign convention here is Q=qx​/q, with q=0 and qt​=qxx​. Indeed qt​/q=Qx​+Q2, so
Qt​=∂x​(Qx​+Q2)=Qxx​+2QQx​.
(88)
Conversely a solution Q determines a locally nonzero q through qx​=Qq, qt​=(Qx​+Q2)q; their compatibility is this Burgers equation. A spatially constant term can be removed by rescaling q in time.
Set μ=qψ in the heat-equation pair. Division by q gives
ψx​+(Q−ik)ψ=1,ψt​+(Qx​+Q2+k2)ψ=Q+ik.​
(89)
Their compatibility can be checked without referring back to q: writing A=ik−Q, B=−Qx​−Q2−k2, we have ψx​=Aψ+1, ψt​=Bψ+Q+ik. The coefficient of ψ in ψxt​−ψtx​ is −Qt​+Qxx​+2QQx​, and the constant term is (ik−Q)(Q+ik)−Qx​−B=0. Thus this linear auxiliary pair is compatible exactly for the required viscous Burgers equation. As in part (a), adjoining a constant component turns it into a homogeneous 2×2 matrix Lax pair.

32D (Principles of Quantum Mechanics)

Words: 174 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 174
32D OurBigBook.com
Generalized position eigenstates satisfy ⟨x∣x′⟩=δ(x−x′) and ∫∣x⟩⟨x∣dx=I. Define the position-space wavefunction ψ(x)=⟨x∣ψ⟩. Completeness then gives ⟨ψ∣ψ⟩=∫∣ψ(x)∣2dx. Position acts by multiplication, ⟨x∣x∣ψ⟩=xψ(x). Using ⟨x∣p⟩=(2πℏ)−1/2eipx/ℏ and momentum completeness, differentiating the Fourier integral gives ⟨x∣p​∣ψ⟩=−iℏψ′(x) on the momentum operator's domain.
For the unit-mass, unit-frequency oscillator define
a=2ℏ​x+ip​​,a†=2ℏ​x−ip​​,[a,a†]=1,H=ℏ(a†a+1/2).
(92)
Since [H,a]=−ℏa, a simultaneous energy eigenstate and a-eigenstate would satisfy [H,a]∣ψα​⟩=0=−ℏα∣ψα​⟩, forcing α=0. For α=0, the energy is ℏ/2, the smallest possible because ⟨a†a⟩=∥aψ∥2≥0.
The position-space equation is (x+ℏ∂x​)ψα​=2ℏ​αψα​. Solving and normalizing, with α=u+iv, gives up to a constant phase
ψα​(x)=(πℏ)−1/4exp[−2ℏ(x−2ℏ​u)2​+iℏ2​​vx].​
(93)
Its squared modulus is a normalized Gaussian, so every complex α gives a normalizable coherent state.
For a creation eigenstate, (x−ℏ∂x​)ψ=2ℏ​βψ instead gives ψ=Cexp[x2/(2ℏ)−2/ℏ​βx]. Every nonzero such function grows quadratically exponentially at infinity and fails square integrability. Hence there are no nonzero normalizable eigenstates of a†. This last symbol is a† in the original PDF, although the converted TeX drops its dagger.

For unit incident plane-wave amplitude, define the scattering amplitude by ψ∼eikz+f(θ)eikr/r at large r. Comparing outgoing radial flux with incident flux gives dσ/dΩ=∣f(θ)∣2. Outside the potential, a real regular radial solution is proportional to jℓ​(kr)cosδℓ​−nℓ​(kr)sinδℓ​, with asymptotic phase sin(kr−ℓπ/2+δℓ​)/(kr). This defines the scattering phase shift modulo π.
The incident plane-wave expansion supplies coefficient (2ℓ+1)iℓ for jℓ​Pℓ​. To preserve its incoming part, replace jℓ​ by eiδℓ​(jℓ​cosδℓ​−nℓ​sinδℓ​). Writing the asymptotic sine in exponentials shows that its incoming coefficient is unchanged and its outgoing coefficient is multiplied by e2iδℓ​. The outgoing difference from the plane wave therefore gives
f(θ)=2ik1​ℓ≥0∑​(2ℓ+1)(e2iδℓ​−1)Pℓ​(cosθ)=k1​ℓ≥0∑​(2ℓ+1)eiδℓ​sinδℓ​Pℓ​(cosθ).​
(94)
Put ρ=ka, t=tanδℓ​, and abbreviate j=jℓ​(ρ), n=nℓ​(ρ). Logarithmic-derivative matching gives aRℓ′​(a)/Rℓ​(a)=ρ(j′−tn′)/(j−tn). The supplied asymptotics determine the constant Wronskian: ρ2(jn′−j′n)=1. Consequently
Qℓ​=ρ(j−tnj′−tn′​−jj′​)=ρj(j−tn)−t​.
(95)
Solving for t gives
tanδℓ​=Qℓ​nℓ​(ka)jℓ​(ka)ka−1Qℓ​jℓ​(ka)2ka​.​
(96)
At zeros of denominators it is interpreted by limits; the logarithmic-derivative definition itself presumes its stated denominators nonzero.
Near a dominant resonant partial wave, sin2δℓ​≈γ2/[(k−k0​)2+γ2]. Neglecting the small other partial waves yields
dΩdσ​≈k2(2ℓ+1)2​(k−k0​)2+γ2γ2​Pℓ​(cosθ)2.​
(97)
This is a resonant peak of width 2∣γ∣ in k, with the partial-wave angular pattern and maximum allowed sin2δℓ​=1 at resonance. Integrating gives σ≈4π(2ℓ+1)γ2/[k2((k−k0​)2+γ2)]. A small background may matter at angular zeros of the dominant wave.

Use rationalized electromagnetic units with c=1 and electrostatic constant 1/(4π). The four-potential Aa=(φ,Ax​,Ay​,Az​) transforms by the same matrix as the coordinates:
φ′=γ(φ−vAx​),Ax′​=γ(Ax​−vφ),Ay′​=Ay​,Az′​=Az​.​
(98)
Write r=y2+z2​ and er​=(0,y,z)/r. Gauss's law for the line at rest gives E′=σer​/(2πr), B′=0. A suitable potential is φ′=−σlog(r/r∗​)/(2π), A′=0. The inverse Lorentz transformation gives φ=γφ′, Ax​=γvφ′. The fields from E=−∇φ−∂t​A and B=∇×A are therefore
E=2πrγσ​er​,B=2πrγvσ​ex​×er​.​
(99)
The sign agrees with a line charge moving in the positive x direction: its density is γσ and its current γvσ. In SI units insert 1/ϵ0​ in the electric expressions and replace B=v×E by B=v×E/c2.
The two invariants check explicitly:
E⋅B=0=E′⋅B′,E2−B2=γ2(1−v2)4π2r2σ2​=E′2−B′2.
(100)
For ∣v∣≪1, the electric field differs from the static field only at order v2, while the magnetic field is of order v and is the field of the moving line current. These fields are evaluated off the charged axis.

Words: 109 Articles: 1

Solution

35A OurBigBook.com
For a scalar, ∇a​ϕ=∂a​ϕ, while its second covariant derivative is ∇a​∇b​ϕ=∂a​∂b​ϕ−Γabc​∂c​ϕ. Partial derivatives commute and the Levi-Civita connection is torsion-free, Γabc​=Γbac​, proving the asserted symmetry.
Write the Einstein equation without cosmological constant as Gab​=κTab​, κ=8πG/c4. Tracing the given Ricci equation gives R=gab∂a​ϕ∂b​ϕ. Hence
Tab​=κ−1(∂a​ϕ∂b​ϕ−21​gab​∂c​ϕ∂cϕ).​
(101)
In units κ=1 the prefactor is absent. Metric compatibility, the product rule and the just-proved symmetric Hessian of a scalar field give
κ∇aTab​=(∇a∇a​ϕ)∂b​ϕ+∂aϕ∇a​∂b​ϕ−∂aϕ∇b​∂a​ϕ=(∇a∇a​ϕ)∂b​ϕ.
(102)
The contracted Bianchi identity makes the left side zero. Wherever the gradient covector is nonzero, at least one component is nonzero, forcing ∇a​∇aϕ=0, even when that gradient is null.
Finally Γaba​=∂b​log−g​, obtained by differentiating the metric determinant. Thus for any vector V, ∇a​Va=(−g​)−1∂a​(−g​Va). Applying it to Va=gab∂b​ϕ proves
∂a​(−g​gab∂b​ϕ)=0.​
(103)

36B (Fluid Dynamics II)

Words: 255 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 255
36B OurBigBook.com
For a material interface with no mass transfer, the normal fluid velocity on both sides equals the interface's normal velocity. For ordinary viscous fluids without interfacial slip, tangential velocities also agree. The stress tensors Ti​=−pi​I+μi​(∇ui​+∇uiT​) have continuous tangential traction when surface tension is uniform; their normal traction jump balances surface-tension curvature. Nonuniform surface tension instead supplies a tangential Marangoni stress. These conditions express conservation of mass, no slip between the contacting fluids and force balance at the interface. For a flat interface of constant tension the full traction is continuous.
Choose x down the plane and y perpendicular outward from it. A steady parallel solution has velocity (u(y),0) and equations
0=−px​+μu′′+ρgsinθ,0=−py​−ρgcosθ.
(104)
For a uniform free layer, px​=0, u(0)=0, u′(h)=0 and p(h)=patm​. Integration gives
p=patm​+ρgcosθ(h−y),u=μρgsinθ​(hy−2y2​).​
(105)
Its flux per unit cross-slope width is
∫0h​u(y)dy=3μρgh3sinθ​.​
(106)
For the two-layer falling film of equal-density viscous fluids let H=(1+α)h and A=ρgsinθ/μ. Equal density gives the same continuous hydrostatic pressure in both, p=patm​+ρgcosθ(H−y). The wall condition is u1​(0)=0, the upper condition u2′​(H)=0, and at h we require u1​=u2​, μu1′​=βμu2′​. Integrating the two momentum equations with these conditions gives
u1​(y)=A(Hy−2y2​),0≤y≤h,​
(107)
u2​(h+z)=Ah2(α+21​)+βA​(αhz−2z2​),0≤z≤αh.​
(108)
The shear stress transmitted to the lower layer is the upper layer's downslope weight per unit area, ρgαhsinθ, obtained by integrating the upper momentum balance from its stress-free surface. It depends on thickness but not upper viscosity. Changing β changes the upper shear rate needed to transmit that stress, while the lower profile depends on α alone.

37C (Waves)

37C OurBigBook.com
For the reflection of a P-wave from a rigid plane, use the displacement convention ux​=ϕx​+ψy​, uy​=ϕy​−ψx​, where ϕ is the P potential and ψ the SV potential. Put ω=kcp​, κ=ksinθ, a=kcosθ, and b=ω2/cs2​−κ2​. The reflected waves must share the tangential wavenumber and frequency and propagate towards negative y, so write
ϕR​=Aei(κx−ay−ωt),ψR​=Bei(κx−by−ωt).
(109)
The rigid barrier requires both displacement components to vanish. On y=0 this gives κ(1+A)−bB=0 and a(1−A)−κB=0. Solving,
A=ab+κ2ab−κ2​,B=ab+κ22aκ​.​
(110)
The total P potential is the given incident wave plus ϕR​, and the S potential is ψR​. Reversing the sign convention for ψ reverses B but leaves the displacement unchanged. At normal incidence A=1,B=0.
An evanescent reflected S wave would require b2<0, or sinθ>cp​/cs​. In a stable isotropic elastic solid cp​>cs​, so this is impossible for real incidence angles: b2=k2[(cp​/cs​)2−sin2θ]>0. The reflected S wave is never evanescent in the physical isotropic case. The inequality identifies the hypothetical critical-angle case if the speed ordering were reversed; it is S-to-P conversion, not this P-to-S conversion, that can become evanescent in an ordinary solid.

x(k+1)=x(k)+ωD−1(b−Ax(k))=(I−ωD−1A)x(k)+ωD−1b.​
(111)
Each new component uses only the previous iterate's components; ω=1 is ordinary Jacobi iteration. Errors evolve by e(k+1)=(I−ωD−1A)e(k).

Solution

Positive definiteness of A implies D>0. Let B=D−1/2AD−1/2, a symmetric positive definite matrix. The additional hypothesis says 2I−B=D−1/2(2D−A)D−1/2>0, so all eigenvalues λ of B satisfy 0<λ<2. The ordinary Jacobi error matrix I−D−1A is similar to I−B and therefore has eigenvalues 1−λ∈(−1,1). Its spectral radius is less than one. The convergence criterion for stationary linear iterations consequently gives convergence from every starting vector.

For an n×n matrix here, D=I. The sine vectors vj​(i)=sin(ijπ/(n+1)) give eigenvalues
λj​=1+21​cosn+1jπ​,1≤j≤n.
(112)
Thus every eigenvalue lies strictly between 1/2 and 3/2. For 0<ω≤4/3, 0<ωλj​<2, so ∣1−ωλj​∣<1, including the upper endpoint ω=4/3. Hence the iteration converges for the entire stated range.
The extreme eigenvalues are 1−a and 1+a, with a=21​cos(π/(n+1)). The spectral radius is max(∣1−ω(1−a)∣,∣1−ω(1+a)∣)=∣1−ω∣+aω for ω>0. It decreases up to one and increases after one, since 0≤a<1. Therefore
ωopt​=1,ρopt​=21​cosn+1π​.​

For n=1 the same formula gives zero spectral radius and exact solution in one ordinary Jacobi step.
